title: How the Australian dollar is set

match.reason: No point in the bank covers how a floating exchange rate is set by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market; e-govtrade only mentions a weaker currency's effect on net exports, so this needs a new point.

draft.title: How the Australian dollar is set
card: The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, such as how many US dollars one Australian dollar buys. The foreign exchange (forex) market is where currencies are bought and sold.
The Australian dollar floats. Its value is set by supply and demand in the forex market, not fixed by the government or the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA).
Foreign buyers need Australian dollars to buy our exports, invest here or travel here. More demand for Australian dollars, with supply unchanged, pushes the dollar's value up.
Australians supply Australian dollars when they swap them for foreign currency to buy imports, invest overseas or travel abroad. More supply, with demand unchanged, pushes the value down.
draft.remember: A floating dollar's price comes from buyers and sellers in the forex market.

a.q: Why is the value of the Australian dollar not set by the government?
opts: It floats, so supply and demand set its value
It is fixed to a basket of other currencies
The RBA sets it each day to match inflation
Exporters and importers agree on it each year
a.why: A floating currency is priced by buyers and sellers in the forex market. The RBA does not set it, and no basket or yearly agreement fixes it.
a.clue: Think about who trades in the forex market.

b.q: Many overseas tourists plan trips to Australia and swap their own currencies for Australian dollars. With nothing else changed, what happens to the Australian dollar?
opts: Demand for it rises, so its value tends to rise
Supply of it rises, so its value tends to fall
Demand for it falls, so its value tends to fall
Supply of it falls, so its value tends to rise
b.why: Tourists must buy Australian dollars to pay for their trips, so demand for the dollar rises and its value tends to rise. It is tempting to call this extra supply, but supply comes from Australians selling dollars for foreign currency.
b.clue: Who is buying Australian dollars here?

a.best: It floats, so supply and demand set its value

b.best: Demand for it rises, so its value tends to rise
